executive_summary: The defining thread of today's content is the accelerating institutional disruption driven by concentrated executive power, most visibly in Washington's breaking news but resonating across the day's broader coverage. Defense Secretary Pete Hegseth's removal of female and Black Navy officers from a promotion list represents a direct, deliberate dismantling of established institutional norms — a pattern that connects to The Economist's question about whether public markets can absorb AI giants like Anthropic and OpenAI, companies whose unchecked scale similarly challenges the institutional frameworks designed to govern them. In both cases, the central tension is the same: legacy structures built for stability and broad accountability are being outpaced or overridden by actors — political or corporate — with the power and will to rewrite the rules unilaterally. This matters because institutional erosion, whether in military promotion protocols or financial market architecture, compounds quietly until the guardrails are gone entirely. Today's signals, taken together, suggest that disruption is no longer a technology story or a politics story in isolation — it is the dominant operating condition across American institutions.

newsletters.title: 🔴 Inside Economics: The left’s new favourite economist

items.headline: Inside Economics: A conversation with the left's new favourite economist
items.blurb: Gabriel Zucman is a controversial economist. In the past few years he has arguably seized the mantle from Thomas Piketty, his fellow Frenchman and co-author, to become the favourite economist of left-wingers everywhere. While fighting battles with other academics about the accuracy of his voluminous data on inequality, he has relentlessly campaigned for taxes on wealth and advised left-wing politicians from Elizabeth Warren to Luiz Inácio Lula da Silva. A few years ago he won the John Bates Clark medal, awarded annually to the best economist under the age of 40. The meat of our discussion on this occasion was about Mr Zucman's new short book "We Need to Tax Billionaires", which takes aim at one specific tax strategy the ultra-rich often use: keeping their wealth in holding companies, such that returns do not generate taxable income.

items.headline: The GOAT returns
items.blurb: Serena Williams, the 23-time Grand Slam singles champion and GOAT of women's tennis, will return to the sport four years after she announced that she was evolving away from it. Williams, 44, will play women's doubles at Queen's, a prestigious grass tournament in southwest London that acts as a warmup for Wimbledon. Williams will partner with Victoria Mboko, the 19-year-old Canadian who stormed into the WTA top 10 last year.

items.headline: An instructive nighttime duel
items.blurb: Naomi Osaka's fashion statements have caused such a stir at the French Open that the four-time Grand Slam champion spends nearly as much time talking about her skirts as she does her tennis. The 28-year-old Osaka walked onto Court Philippe-Chatrier for her fourth-round duel with world No. 1 Aryna Sabalenka on Monday in a tulle-and-sequin skirt that extended her gold, sequined match dress all the way to the red clay. She walked off it on the end of a compelling but clarifying 7-5, 6-3 defeat. It showed how important Osaka and Sabalenka's star power is to tennis. But it also showed how far Sabalenka, Iga Świątek and their peers have taken tennis since Osaka's star was at its height a little over five years ago.

items.headline: A.J. Brown Watch: Why the timing matters
items.blurb: With the calendar flipping to June 1, the Eagles can finally trade A.J. Brown to the Patriots. Daniel Popper published a detailed explainer on why teams wait until today, the very important date of June 1, to finalize a deal. If Brown is traded by the Eagles before 4 p.m. ET today, league rules force Philly to account for Brown's remaining bonus money in the 2026 league year. If they instead trade Brown after 4 p.m. today, the Eagles can divide that money over two seasons.

items.headline: Myles Garrett Traded: Browns and Rams
items.blurb: Cap-starved Cleveland would be on the hook for all of his $41.09 million signing bonus if it officially moved him before today, but can spread that amount across two seasons by processing the trade after 4 p.m. In March, the team and Garrett agreed to a contract modification that deferred a total of $29 million in bonus payments due to Garrett over the next three years. The only real explanation for the modification is that both sides were at least opening a trade window.

If they do, the three giga-IPOs could add as much as $4trn to the market value of listed American companies in a matter of months. Can the stockmarket handle this? Probably—but in the longer term, expect some indigestion.

items.headline: Welcome to Evanston, where woke never died
items.blurb: In America, the idea of paying reparations to victims of racism is not new: five states and some cities have launched exploratory commissions. But only one scheme has actually paid out money. Our correspondent reports from Evanston, a Chicago suburb home to Northwestern University. Its proponents hope it will inspire something bigger, but the scheme is faltering.

breaking_digest.narrative:
Several significant developments emerged from Washington on Monday. Defense Secretary Pete Hegseth removed female and Black Navy officers from a scheduled promotion list [2], a move that drew immediate scrutiny as a rollback of diversity policies within the military. Separately, President Trump is said to be backing away from a proposed $1.8 billion payout fund, the details of which remain under discussion [1]. Together, the two stories underscore an ongoing pattern of policy reversals and personnel decisions reshaping federal institutions.

On the media front, veteran CBS News correspondent Scott Pelley publicly accused CBS News leadership of "murdering" the flagship newsmagazine "60 Minutes" [3], a remarkable on-the-record rebuke that signals deepening turmoil at one of broadcast journalism's most storied programs. In the business world, AI company Anthropic filed to go public, setting the stage for what could be one of the year's most closely watched initial public offerings in the technology sector [4]. Finally, Serena Williams announced she will return to competitive tennis to play Queen's doubles [5], her most significant step back onto the court since her retirement.
